title-group.article-title: Catchment-Specific Drivers of Microplastic Contamination in Two Central European Rivers: A Citizen Science Monitoring Campaign Along the Neckar and the Lusatian Neisse

abstract.p: Understanding microplastic (MP) transport dynamics in river systems requires spatially and temporally resolved monitoring to disentangle localized point sources from diffuse catchment inputs. This study investigated MP contamination across two contrasting Central European catchments: the heavily impounded, industrialized Neckar (n = 136; June 2026) and the transboundary Lusatian Neisse (n = 102; March and May 2026). A standardized monitoring campaign collected 0.5 L grab samples across both rivers and at the Neckar–Rhine confluence in Mannheim, including an inland port area, where 12 sites were sampled on four dates between January and April 2026. Samples underwent hydrogen peroxide digestion, fluorescent staining with a MP-specific dye mixture (particles > 10 µm), automated fluorescence microscopy, and geospatial analysis incorporating land cover and wastewater infrastructure metrics. Microplastic concentrations were significantly higher in the Neisse than in the Neckar (median 22.5 vs. 5.0 MP L−1; Cliff’s delta = 0.44). Because the two rivers were sampled in different months and at different water levels, seasonal and hydrological contributions to this difference cannot be excluded. In the Mannheim port area, the highest site mean was recorded upstream of a lock structure (544 MP L−1) with pronounced temporal variability at this site (5 to 1591 MP L−1). Neither local land use nor wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) metrics showed a detectable association with MP abundances in either river under the present design, which could reliably detect only moderate to strong associations. These results indicate that immediate land cover and WWTP proximity left no detectable signal in surface-water MP concentrations, possibly because point-source signals are masked by diffuse inputs, hydrological dynamics and temporal variation. Concentrations in the Neisse decreased from the upper to the lower reaches; whether this reflects the secondary WWTPs of the upper catchment or other longitudinal differences (e.g., flow conditions) could not be resolved.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Plastics have become indispensable to modern society, and the steady growth in global production has meant that plastic debris is now detectable in virtually every environmental compartment [1,2]. Particular attention is paid to microplastics (MPs), conventionally defined as plastic particles smaller than 5 mm, which are either manufactured as primary particles or formed through the mechanical, photochemical and biological fragmentation of larger plastic items [2,3]. Because of their persistence, their ubiquity and their small size, which allows uptake by a wide range of aquatic organisms, MPs are now regarded as a contaminant class of considerable ecological relevance [4,5]. Documented effects include physical damage to the digestive tract and altered growth and reproduction [5,6]. Further, MPs act as vectors for sorbed organic pollutants and heavy metals and can release monomers, plastic additives and volatile organic compounds into the environment [7,8].

For a long time, research focused on marine systems, and inland waters were regarded primarily as transport corridors. Modeling studies have shown, however, that rivers are not only pathways but also sinks and reaction spaces in their own right: an estimated 0.5 million tons of plastic reach the seas via rivers each year, with emissions strongly concentrated in a limited number of catchments [9,10,11]. At the same time, a substantial share of the plastic entering a river system is retained within it, in bed sediments, on embankments and in floodplains [12,13]. Rivers are therefore themselves contaminated ecosystems whose assessment cannot be reduced to a load calculation at the river mouth [10,14].

The database for freshwater systems nevertheless remains fragmentary, primarily for methodological reasons. Sampling, sample preparation and identification of MPs are labor-, time- and cost-intensive: field sampling is typically followed by sieving, oxidative removal of the organic matrix, density separation and finally polymer-specific identification by µ-FTIR, Raman or pyrolysis GC-MS [15,16]. The effort required per sample limits, in practice, the number of samples that can be processed so that many studies are confined to a few grab samples at a few stations [10,17]. Standardization is also still inadequate: mesh sizes, lower size cut-offs, sample volumes, reporting units (particles m−3 vs. particles L−1 vs. mass concentration) and quality-assurance measures differ so strongly between studies that a direct comparison of published concentrations is frequently not meaningful [16,17,18].

A second, frequently underestimated problem is the high spatio-temporal variability of MP in rivers. Concentrations fluctuate with discharge, precipitation events, resuspension and seasonal patterns of use, so that single measurements are rarely representative [13,18,19]. The direction of these dependencies is contested: while some studies report positive relationships between discharge and MP load through mobilization and resuspension [13], others document dilution with increasing discharge or no robust relationship at all [12,20]. Whether and to what extent particles settle depends in turn on polymer density and particle shape as well as on aging, aggregation and biofilm formation, which can alter effective density during transport [21]. The consequence is clear: only comprehensive, repeated campaigns with high spatial and temporal resolution permit robust statements on contamination levels and trends [17,18,22].

Such datasets are simultaneously the prerequisite for hotspot and source analysis. Point sources, in particular wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) effluents, stormwater overflows, industrial discharges and plastics-processing sites, can only be identified if closely spaced measurements are taken upstream and downstream of candidate sources [10,23]. The relative importance of point versus diffuse sources varies strongly by region and is assessed controversially [10]. Linking measured concentrations with spatial information on land cover, population density and infrastructure is therefore necessary to attribute sources and sinks reliably [10,24].

Only on this basis can the actual ecological burden be estimated. Approaches to risk assessment via the pollution load index, polymer hazard index, or the comparison of measured concentrations with ecotoxicological effect thresholds presuppose spatially resolved, methodologically consistent data [1]. Finally, reliable measurements are the basis for mitigation measures and their verification and for legislation and its enforcement, for instance under the EU Water Framework Directive and the recast Urban Wastewater Treatment Directive, which foresees regular MP monitoring for larger treatment plants [23,25,26].

One route out of the conflict between analytical effort and required data density is to combine simplified, standardized sampling with broad participation by volunteers. Simplified sampling systems have already been deployed successfully in difficult-to-access running waters, and standardized monitoring protocols for rivers are now available [27]. Citizen science approaches offer the potential to increase spatial and temporal coverage substantially; their application to MP monitoring in rivers has, however, hardly been tested systematically, and safeguarding data quality, particularly contamination control, remains a central challenge [17].

Against this background, the present study reports a comprehensive, spatially and temporally resolved MP monitoring campaign for two Central European river systems with markedly different catchment characteristics. The Lusatian Neisse (Lužická Nisa/Nysa Łużycka) runs 246 km from its source in the Jizera Mountains to its confluence with the Oder, passing the conurbations of Liberec, Jablonec, Zittau and Görlitz/Zgorzelec [28]. The Neckar runs 362 km from its source near Villingen-Schwenningen through Stuttgart, Heilbronn and Mannheim to its confluence with the Rhine; 203 km of its course, from Plochingen to the Rhine confluence at Mannheim, are regulated by 27 barrages with locks, and it discharges immediately adjacent to one of the largest inland ports in Europe [29,30]. Monitoring was carried out with a citizen science-based approach: 0.5 L grab samples were taken and analyzed for microplastics using a standardized protocol based on fluorescence staining. The two rivers were selected because they represent contrasting catchment types within the same climatic region: a heavily impounded, navigable and densely industrialized river that discharges next to a major inland port (Neckar) and a smaller transboundary river with a textile-industrial legacy, secondary wastewater treatment in its upper reaches and a predominantly rural lower course (Neisse). Both rivers were covered by ongoing citizen-science projects, which made a dense spatial coverage of the entire river courses possible.

The study evaluates the spatial distribution of microplastics along entire river courses using a large number of sampling locations and additionally examines whether distance to upstream wastewater treatment plants and surrounding land-use patterns influence observed concentrations. In the Mannheim confluence and port area, the study also investigates small-scale spatial variability and temporal changes through repeated sampling.

Specifically, the study tested four hypotheses: (H1) MP concentrations differ between the two catchments when sampled and analyzed with the same protocol; (H2) MP concentrations increase with the share of settlement and industrial land in the immediate surroundings of the sampling site; (H3) MP concentrations increase with proximity to, and size of, the nearest upstream WWTP and are higher downstream of plants with a lower treatment level; and (H4) in the Mannheim confluence and port area, temporal variation at a given site is of similar magnitude as the spatial variation between sites. H1 is addressed in Section 3.1, H4 in Section 3.2, H2 in Section 3.3 and H3 in Section 3.4.

sec.title: 2.1. Sampling Sites
sec.p: Sampling was carried out along two Central European rivers, the Neckar in southwestern Germany and the Lusatian Neisse on the German–Polish–Czech border, together with a set of dedicated sites in the industrial harbor of Mannheim.

The Neckar is a 362 km long right-bank tributary of the Rhine in Baden-Württemberg, Germany [30]. It rises near Villingen-Schwenningen in the Schwenninger Moos at an elevation of approximately 706 m and discharges into the Rhine at Mannheim at about 95 m [30]. Along 203 km of its lower and middle course, between Plochingen (Germany) and the mouth at Mannheim (Germany), the river is impounded by 27 barrages with locks that together bridge about 161 m of head and is navigable for inland shipping [29]. The catchment combines forested headwaters in the Black Forest and Swabian Alb foreland with intensively used agricultural land and a succession of densely populated and industrialized conurbations, among them Stuttgart, Heilbronn and Mannheim. The confluence with the Rhine lies immediately adjacent to one of the largest inland ports in Europe.

The Lusatian Neisse (Czech Lužická Nisa, Polish Nysa Łużycka) is a 246 km long left-bank tributary of the Oder draining a transboundary catchment of 4399 km2 shared between Poland (58%), Germany (33%) and the Czech Republic (9%); forest (43.5%) and agricultural land (45%) dominate the catchment, whereas urban and urban–rural areas cover only about 5% [31]. It originates in the Jizera Mountains in the northern Czech Republic and joins the Oder near Ratzdorf, forming the border between Germany and Poland over much of its lower course. Its upper reaches drain the conurbation of Liberec and Jablonec nad Nisou; further downstream the river passes Chrastava, Zittau and the twin city of Görlitz/Zgorzelec before crossing a predominantly rural, agriculturally used lowland. The upper catchment carries a long industrial legacy. Liberec has been a center of cloth-making since the late sixteenth century; from the late eighteenth century onward, its mechanized spinning and weaving mills were sited along the Lusatian Neisse and its tributaries, drawing water power through millraces [28,31,32].

The Mannheim industrial harbor forms part of the Rhine–Neckar port complex at the mouth of the Neckar. It accommodates bulk goods handling, the chemical and plastic processing industry and associated logistics. Within this area, the access channel of the Bonadieshafen harbor basin was sampled as a separate site. The 12 sites of the repeated port campaign are located at the mouth of the Neckar (Neckarspitze), on the Rhine and in the adjoining port basins, channels and lock structures (Friesenheimer Insel, Bonadieshafen, Sandhofen); the supplementary school samples were taken at 15 locations on the lower Neckar, at the confluence and on the Rhine within the city of Mannheim (Supplementary S1).

sec.title: 2.2. Sampling Dates
sec.p: Sampling along the Lusatian Neisse was conducted in two campaigns. A first campaign was carried out in the Görlitz area from 12 to 13 March 2026, during which 15 samples were collected by the municipal utility company (Stadtwerke Görlitz). The main campaign, covering the entire course of the river, followed from 25 to 27 May 2026 and yielded 97 samples collected by Wasser 3.0 staff. In total, 112 samples were obtained from the Neisse. Ten of these samples were taken outside the river channel of the Neisse (two in the Oder downstream of the confluence, four in the Mšeno reservoir and four in a lake near Hrádek nad Nisou) and were excluded, leaving 102 river samples (15 from March, 87 from May; Table 1).

Sampling on the Neckar comprised a longitudinal profile of the main stem and, at the Neckar–Rhine confluence in Mannheim, a repeated port campaign and supplementary school sampling. The longitudinal profile covering the whole course of the Neckar was recorded from 7 to 9 June 2026 and comprised 136 samples. Samples of the Neckar were taken using the citizen science approach by volunteers, schools and universities of applied sciences. All helpers received detailed, illustrated instructions for sample collection, along with the corresponding sample bottles (see Section 2.3) and thermometers. The instructions described the sampling procedure of Section 2.3 (rinsing of the bottle, sampling depth and closing of the bottle) and the recording of each sample in the smartphone app. Including school and university classes, more than 300 people were reached directly in this project. According to the app records of the 136 profile samples, 21% were collected by school and university groups, 36% by individual volunteers and 39% by Wasser 3.0 staff (4% without collector information).

Quality control of the volunteer-collected samples comprised (i) the use of identical, laboratory-supplied amber glass bottles by all collectors; (ii) the recording of GPS position, time, water temperature and a site description for each sample in the app; (iii) a plausibility check of each georeference against the river course and sampling route; (iv) centralized processing and analysis of all samples in one laboratory by trained staff (Section 2.4, Section 2.5 and Section 2.6); and (v) a comparison of the concentrations obtained by the different collector groups, including co-located samples taken on the same day (Section 2.7). Potential sources of error in volunteer sampling include contamination during handling (e.g., from clothing), deviations in sampling depth and in the distance from the bank, inclusion of the surface film or sediment and imprecise georeferences. These error sources were not quantified individually and contribute to the overall variability of the data (Section 4.6).

In addition, the Neckar–Rhine confluence near Mannheim and the inland port area were sampled at 12 sites on four dates (13 January, 9 February, 4 March and 8 April 2026); one sample (site 1, first round) was lost during laboratory processing, resulting in 47 measurements. Furthermore, school groups collected 17 single grab samples at 15 locations along the Neckar, at the confluence and on the Rhine in Mannheim between 30 April and 7 May 2026. The Mannheim data are evaluated separately (Section 3.2) and were not included in the comparison of the two rivers (Section 3.1). For sensitivity analyses of the land-use and WWTP descriptors (Section 3.3 and Section 3.4), the 12 site means of the port campaign and 16 of the school samples (one excluded because of an ambiguous georeference) were added to the Neckar main stem (“Neckar including Mannheim”, n = 164). Table 1 summarizes the number of samples collected, excluded and analyzed.

Sampling frequency varied due to personnel availability, site accessibility and the laboratory capacity available within the project budget. Along the Neisse, the mean distance between neighboring sampling locations was 1.9 km, with a maximum gap of 8.5 km; along the Neckar, the mean spacing was 2.0 km, with a maximum gap of 9.5 km (distances along a simplified river axis, see Section 2.7).

Table 2 lists the water levels at gauges of the three rivers on the sampling dates. During the longitudinal profile of the Neckar, water levels were close to the long-term mean (Heidelberg 216–224 cm vs. 222 cm), whereas the May profile of the Neisse was sampled at water levels below the long-term mean (Görlitz 128–134 cm vs. 161 cm) and the March campaign on the Neisse at elevated water levels (231–242 cm). During the port campaign, the water level of the Rhine at Maxau ranged from 414 to 512 cm (long-term mean 496 cm). The precipitation flag was set for only 1 of the 102 Neisse samples and for none of the Neckar samples and was therefore not used as a covariate.

sec.title: 2.3. Sampling Method
sec.p: Water samples were collected as grab samples using 0.5 L amber glass bottles (Art-No.: 1-1301-0500-54, Rixius GmbH, Mannheim, Germany), with caps made from black PP (Art-No.: 8-1110-54; Rixius GmbH, Mannheim, Germany). At each site the bottle was rinsed three times with river water before it was filled and closed. Until analysis, the samples were kept at room temperature. The maximum time between sampling and sample preparation was 4 weeks. The bottle was submerged by hand from the bank or from a jetty so that sub-surface water was sampled at a depth of approximately 5–10 cm; the surface film was not sampled separately.

Every sampling point was georeferenced by GPS. In addition, water temperature, a binary precipitation flag and a description of the site were recorded for each sample. These data were recorded with a smartphone app designed specifically for this purpose.

sec.title: 2.4. Sample Preparation
sec.p: Sample preparation is based on the method described in [36].

Preparing the samples for MP analysis combined an oxidative digestion of the organic particle fraction by means of hydrogen peroxide with a subsequent fluorescent staining step that renders the MP particles detectable.

In the laboratory each sample was passed over a stainless-steel filter with a 10 µm pore size (Wolftechnik Filtersysteme GmbH & Co. KG, Weil, Germany), resistant to hydrogen peroxide and Fenton’s reagent. The filter carrying the retained solids was transferred into a glass beaker and digested oxidatively with 35% hydrogen peroxide, using iron (II) sulfate (FeSO4·7H2O) as a catalyst. For this purpose, 25–30 mL of hydrogen peroxide (AB171423, abcr GmbH, Karlsruhe, Germany) were poured over the filter, to which 3–5 granules of the solid catalyst (AB203817, abcr GmbH, Karlsruhe, Germany) were then added. Digestion proceeded for 60 min at 80 °C, conditions under which the recovery of polymer particles has been validated for PE, PP, PA, polyester and PVC, with recoveries of 93–102% after digestion and staining (Section 2.5; [36]).

After digestion, the sample, suspended in the hydrogen peroxide, was filtered once more over the stainless-steel filter and rinsed with demineralized water. All solids, including MP, were retained on the filter surface, while the hydrogen peroxide passed into the filtrate. The retained particles from the filter surface were rinsed off into a beaker using deionized water and the volume was filled up to 100 mL.

Staining of the resulting suspension followed, for which abcr eco Wasser 3.0 detect mix MP-1 (AB930015, abcr GmbH, Karlsruhe, Germany), a mixture of newly developed Nile Red derivatives that differs from Nile Red itself in its staining selectivity (Section 4.6) [35], was dosed at 0.25 mg L−1 and heated for 60 min at 80 °C [36]. Following staining, the samples were filtered onto black filter membranes of Ø 25 mm (Metricel® Black PES membrane filter, 0.80 µm, Pall, Dreieich, Germany).

sec.title: 2.5. Fluorescent Imaging and Microplastic Detection
sec.p: MP detection is based on the method described in [36].

Imaging was performed on a Zeiss Axio Zoom.V16 microscope (Carl Zeiss Microscopy Deutschland GmbH, Oberkochen, Germany) equipped with a PlanNeoFluar Z 1.0× objective; images were captured by an Axiocam 712 mono camera [18,36]. Detection in the green fluorescence channel was enabled by a custom filter set supplied by AHF Analysentechnik AG (Tübingen, Germany). The imaging parameters correspond to those specified in Sturm et al. 2025 [18].

The entire Ø 25 mm filter was evaluated for each grab sample. Image processing and particle counting were carried out in ZEN 3.8 (Carl Zeiss Microscopy Deutschland GmbH) using the ZEN Toolkit 2D particle counting module, which identifies microplastic particles automatically on the basis of predefined brightness thresholds specified in [18]. The optical resolution of the setup is 1 µm per pixel. The minimum particle size for detection was set to 10 µm, corresponding to the stainless-steel filters used for sample processing. In relation to the sample volume, the result is reported in MP L−1. Particle sizes and size classes were not determined. Reported concentrations therefore refer to fluorescently stained particles that meet the size and brightness criteria; they were not confirmed spectroscopically (see Section 4.6).

For this method, including sample preparation, recovery rates of 97.5% (PE), 93.3% (PP), 101.7% (PA), 100% (polyester, PES) and 96.7% (PVC) have been reported, whereas natural particles were falsely detected at rates of 5% (wood), 5% (chalk) and 5.8% (chitin) [36]. These validation data refer to the complete procedure applied here (digestion, staining and automated detection).

sec.title: 2.6. Contamination Control
sec.p: Contamination was controlled by confining all MP-related work to a laboratory reserved exclusively for this purpose. Ahead of every preparation session, the room was wiped down with cloths that do not shed lint. Staff entering it wore protective suits of the same fiber-free type (model 4510 M, 3M Deutschland GmbH, Neuss, Germany), which were rolled with an adhesive roller beforehand to keep fiber release to a minimum. An air filtration unit (AC0830, Philips, Amsterdam, The Netherlands) ran continuously to lower the airborne particle load. Glass equipment was used wherever this was practicable to avoid plastic-derived artifacts, and all sample vessels were covered with aluminum foil while being handled and stored. Procedural laboratory blanks were analyzed routinely using the same demineralized water used for sample processing. Each blank passed through the complete procedure (filtration, digestion, staining and detection). To correct for background contamination, each measured microplastic concentration was adjusted by subtracting the mean value of the ten most recent laboratory blanks.

For the Neckar samples, the laboratory blanks averaged 15.4 MP L−1, and for the Neisse samples, 16.9 MP L−1. Because the Neckar and the Neisse samples were processed at different times, each dataset was corrected with the blanks measured during its own processing period. No field or transport blanks were taken; contamination during sampling, transport and storage cannot therefore be excluded (Section 4.6). Concentrations that became zero or negative after blank subtraction were set to 0 MP L−1 and are treated as non-detects in the statistical analysis (Section 2.7).

sec.title: 2.7. Geospatial and Statistical Analysis
sec.p: Spatial and anthropogenic land use analyses were conducted in R (version 4.4.1) using the terra (version 1.9.11) and sf (version 1.0.21) packages by intersecting sampling coordinates with the 2018 CORINE Land Cover (CLC) 100 m raster and the European Environment Agency Urban Wastewater Treatment Plants (UWWTD) database. Local land use was characterized by using circular buffers around each sampling point, where the dominant land use class was identified via the statistical mode within a 300 m radius. The percentage cover of urban fabric and of industrial zones was quantified within a 1 km radius by matching CLC class designations. The urban-fabric criterion captured continuous urban fabric, discontinuous urban fabric and green urban areas (CLC 111, 112, 141); the industrial criterion captured industrial or commercial units (CLC 121) only, so that port areas, airports, road and rail land and dump sites were not counted as industrial cover. CORINE 2018 was the most recent inventory available for this analysis; land-cover changes between 2018 and the 2026 campaigns are expected to be small at the 100 m resolution for the established land uses along both rivers but could not be verified individually.

To assess upstream wastewater pressures, spatial layers were projected into metric UTM coordinate systems (EPSG:32632, zone 32N, for the Neckar and EPSG:32633, zone 33N, for the Lusatian Neisse), and a linear reference axis of the river was established from its geographic source. A linear referencing algorithm calculated the relative distance along the river channel for both the sampling locations and regional WWTPs located within a 30 km buffer of the study area. By comparing these river positions, the closest strictly upstream WWTP was isolated for each sampling site using a nearest-neighbor analysis. For each identified upstream facility, the geodesic distance, nominal design capacity, actual entering population load, and specific purification tier (primary, secondary, or tertiary treatment) were extracted. Because the nearest-plant distance ignores effluent volume and dilution and no paired upstream–downstream samples were taken at individual outfalls, the WWTP analysis is an exploratory screening. It was restricted to samples that are hydraulically connected to the assigned plants, i.e., the Neisse and the Neckar main stem; samples of the Mannheim confluence and port area were used only in sensitivity analyses.

Relationships between MP concentration and individual covariates were examined using Spearman rank correlation, which does not presuppose normally distributed data. Differences in MP concentrations across categorical land-use classes were evaluated using Kruskal–Wallis H tests, with post hoc pairwise comparisons adjusted using the Holm-Bonferroni method. Binary group contrasts (e.g., near-field vs. far-field WWTP proximity, industrial land presence) were tested using Mann–Whitney U tests, with effect sizes calculated via Cliff’s delta. U is reported for the first-named sample (U = R1 − n1(n1 + 1)/2, mid-ranks for ties), with p-values from the tie-corrected normal approximation. Cliff’s delta was computed as delta = P(X > Y) − P(X < Y) = 2U/(n1n2) − 1, which holds irrespective of ties. Because many pairs of samples are tied, mostly at 0 MP L−1, the probability of superiority is reported as A = P(X > Y) + ½P(X = Y) together with P(X > Y), P(X < Y) and P(X = Y); 95% confidence intervals for delta and A were obtained from 10,000 bootstrap resamples. Spearman coefficients are given with 95% confidence intervals (Fisher z transformation, variance 1.06/(n − 3)). Because all non-detects share the lowest rank, rank-based statistics do not depend on the value assigned to non-detects below the lowest detected concentration. Holm adjustment was applied within each family of comparisons: the ten pairwise Dunn tests among the five land-use classes and the covariate coefficients of each count model; the ten main correlations of Section 3.3 and Section 3.4 (five descriptors in two rivers) are reported with unadjusted p-values, none of which would remain significant after Holm adjustment across this family. “Significant” denotes statistical significance at α = 0.05; effect sizes are reported with 95% confidence intervals.

To address spatial confounding between WWTP treatment tier and longitudinal position in the Neisse, three complementary controls were applied: partial Spearman correlation controlling for distance from source, spatial restriction to the co-occurring 0–60 km upstream reach, and multivariable modeling. Sensitivity analyses repeated the land-use and WWTP tests with the Mannheim samples added to the Neckar main stem (Neckar including Mannheim, n = 164).

The joint effect of the covariates was first assessed by a multiple linear regression of log10(MP + 1), i.e., with a constant of 1 MP L−1 added before the log transform (predictors: settlement and industrial land-cover share, distance to and population served by the nearest upstream WWTP, and catchment identity; HC3 standard errors); its sensitivity to the added constant was examined for constants from 0.1 to 10 MP L−1. Because the zeros make any such constant arbitrary and catchment identity merely restates the difference between the two rivers, covariate effects were then estimated separately for each catchment with count models: a negative binomial (NB2) generalized linear model with log link and a hurdle model (logistic model for detection, zero-truncated NB2 model for positive values), both fitted by maximum likelihood to the reported blank-corrected concentrations (integer particles per liter). As the nominal sample volume (0.5 L) was identical for all river samples, a volume offset is constant and absorbed by the intercept; refitting to particle numbers per bottle with log(0.5 L) as offset changed the rate ratios by less than 2.5%. Predictors were settlement and industrial share, log10 distance to and log10 population served by the nearest upstream WWTP, along-river position and, for the Neisse, the campaign (March vs. May). Models were compared by AIC; multicollinearity was checked with variance inflation factors and the residuals of the corresponding log-linear models with Shapiro–Wilk and studentized Breusch–Pagan tests. An identical set of covariates and an identical analytical procedure were applied to both rivers so that the two catchments remain directly comparable. A significance level of p < 0.05 was adopted throughout.

Spatial dependence along each river was assessed on an approximate along-river coordinate, obtained by projecting every sampling point onto an ordered polyline through georeferenced sites from source to mouth. Moran’s I of log10(MP + 1) and of model residuals was computed with row-standardized weights for neighbors within 2, 5 and 10 km along the river and tested with 9999 permutations; empirical correlograms and semivariograms were computed for distance classes up to 80 km. Generalized least squares (GLS) models with an exponential correlation structure and a nugget were compared with independent-error models by likelihood ratio, and cluster-robust standard errors with river reaches of 2, 5 and 10 km as clusters were computed for the count models. The river comparison was repeated with a moving-block bootstrap (blocks of 5, 10 and 20 km) and on reach-level medians. The repeated port measurements were analyzed with a negative binomial mixed model with site as random intercept and sampling round as fixed effect (maximum likelihood, Gauss–Hermite quadrature), complemented by Friedman and Kruskal–Wallis tests; 95% confidence intervals of site means reflecting Poisson counting error were derived from the total particle number per site.

Minimum detectable correlations were computed for α = 0.05 (two-sided) and 80% power from Fisher’s z (variance 1/(n − 3) for Pearson and 1.06/(n − 3) for Spearman coefficients), for the nominal sample size and for an effective sample size accounting for along-river autocorrelation of both variables (neff = 1 + n2/tr(RxRy)). A simulation (1500 replicates per effect size) quantified the additional attenuation caused by Poisson counting error at the observed particle numbers per bottle and by excess zeros, using zero-inflated Poisson–lognormal models fitted to each river. Concentrations of samples taken by Wasser 3.0 staff, school and university groups and individual volunteers were compared with a Kruskal–Wallis test, and co-located samples (≤0.5 km apart, same day) taken by staff and by other collectors with a Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Statistical computations were performed in Python 3.12 (NumPy 2.4, SciPy 1.17, pandas 3.0); count, hurdle, mixed and GLS models were fitted by maximum likelihood with SciPy optimization routines and standard errors from the numerical Hessian. The full statistical output is provided in the Supplementary Materials.

sec.title: 3.1. Comparison of MP Concentrations in the Neisse and the Neckar
sec.p: The results of the MP monitoring (Table 3; Figure 1) of the Neckar main stem (n = 136) and the Neisse (n = 102) show heavily right-skewed distributions with substantial dispersion relative to their means.

The Neckar main stem displays a mean concentration of 19.4 MP L−1 (S.D. 54.0) and a median of 5.0 MP L−1. In contrast, the Neisse shows an almost three times higher mean of 55.4 MP L−1 (S.D. 87.5) and a 4.5 times higher median of 22.5 MP L−1. The Mann–Whitney U (Wilcoxon rank-sum) test showed a significant difference between the two rivers (U = 9953.5 for the Neisse sample, n1 = 102, n2 = 136, z = 5.81, p < 0.001; Hodges–Lehmann shift 12 MP L−1, 95% CI 8–20 MP L−1). The effect size is medium to large (Cliff’s delta = 2U/(n1n2) − 1 = 0.44, 95% CI 0.30–0.56). As 6.3% of all sample pairs are tied, almost all of them at 0 MP L−1, the probability of superiority is stated explicitly: a randomly drawn Neisse sample exceeds a randomly drawn Neckar sample in 68.6% of pairings, is lower in 25.1% and equal in 6.3%, i.e., A = P(X > Y) + ½P(X = Y) = 0.72 (95% CI 0.65–0.78). The difference is robust to the dataset definition (Neckar including Mannheim, n = 164: U = 11,337, delta = 0.36, A = 0.68, p < 0.001; Neisse May campaign only: delta = 0.45) and to along-river dependence between samples (Section 3.5). Because the two rivers were sampled in different months and at different water levels (Table 2), this difference characterizes the two sampling campaigns and cannot be attributed to catchment characteristics alone (Section 4.2).

The percentile comparison shows that concentrations in the Neisse are consistently higher than in the Neckar across the entire distribution. While both rivers share identical lower percentiles (P5 and P10 = 0 MP L−1), the Neisse begins to diverge at P25 and exceeds the Neckar more strongly toward the upper tail. Median values already differ markedly (22.5 vs. 5.0 MP L−1), and the absolute gap widens at higher percentiles, with the Neisse reaching about 3.5 to 4 times the Neckar value at P75, P90 and P95 (60.8 vs. 17.3, 131 vs. 34 and 242 vs. 69 MP L−1). The inter-percentile distances further highlight this pattern: the P25–P75 range is 17.3 MP L−1 for the Neckar but 53.5 MP L−1 for the Neisse, and the P10–P90 range expands from 34 MP L−1 in the Neckar to 131 MP L−1 in the Neisse.

sec.title: 3.2. Spatial and Temporal Dynamics of Microplastic Contamination in the Neckar–Rhine Confluence and Surrounding Port Infrastructure
sec.p: Repeated monitoring across the port infrastructure surrounding the Neckar–Rhine confluence in Mannheim revealed high spatial heterogeneity in microplastic (MP) contamination on a small scale (Figure 2, Table 4). Mean concentrations ranged from 11 MP L−1 at the Diffené Bridge to a pronounced peak of 544 MP L−1 upstream of the Bonadieshafen lock. This site had the highest mean concentration; however, given the large variation between sampling rounds, the differences between sites were not statistically significant (Kruskal–Wallis H = 8.07, df = 11, p = 0.71). Additional elevated contamination levels exceeding 100 MP L−1 were recorded at other sites within the port infrastructure, specifically near the recycling center on the Friesenheimer Insel (167 MP L−1) and at the terminal section near the Sandhofen ferry (126 MP L−1). These spatial contrasts may reflect a combination of localized terrestrial input sources and hydrodynamically induced retention effects typical of artificial port basins.

In addition to these spatial patterns, the contamination profiles exhibit intense temporal dynamics that complicate environmental risk assessments within the confluence zone. Upstream of the Bonadieshafen lock, for instance, the MP concentration varied drastically over time, ranging from 5 MP L−1 on 4 March 2026 to 1591 MP L−1 on 8 April 2026. Conducting only a single, discrete sampling event during low-exposure periods would fail to capture these temporal dynamics, leading to a severe underestimation of the actual contamination within the port and confluence system.

Across all port sites, the sampling rounds did not differ systematically (Friedman test on the 11 sites with four rounds, χ2 = 1.75, df = 3, p = 0.63; round medians 72, 11, 36 and 8 MP L−1). In a negative binomial mixed model with site as random intercept and round as fixed effect, neither the between-site variance (standard deviation 0.73 on the log scale; likelihood-ratio test p = 0.12) nor the round effect (p = 0.52) was significant; the intraclass correlation was 0.29, i.e., most of the variation occurred between repeated measurements at the same site. The 17 supplementary school samples (30 April–7 May 2026) ranged from 0 to 2853 MP L−1 (median 8.7 MP L−1); the two samples taken at the Neckarspitze on 5 May 2026 (3.3 and 2853 MP L−1) illustrate the extreme short-term variability at the confluence.

sec.title: 3.3. Influence of Land Use on MP Contamination
sec.p: Land use in the immediate surroundings of the sampling points, the dominant CORINE class within 300 m and the settlement and industry shares within 1 km, showed no detectable influence on microplastic contamination in either catchment (Figure 3). In the Lusatian Neisse, particle abundances remained uniform across all land-cover categories (Kruskal–Wallis H = 0.20, df = 3, p = 0.98; four classes with n ≥ 4, the water-body class n = 2 excluded), with nearly identical median concentrations (16.5 to 24.0 MP L−1) observed across urban, agricultural, forest, and industrial settings. On the Neckar main stem, no difference between land-cover classes was detected either (H = 5.64, df = 4, p = 0.23). Only when the Mannheim samples were added (Neckar including Mannheim, n = 164) did the classes differ (H = 11.34, df = 4, p = 0.023), with the forest/semi-natural class lower than the industrial/transport class (Dunn test, Holm-adjusted p = 0.036). This indicates that the apparent land-use effect reflects the concentration step between the main stem and the confluence and port area rather than a land-cover signal along the river; a formal interaction test was not performed.

Furthermore, no statistically significant link between adjacent land use and riverine contamination was found. Neither the proportion of settlement (Spearman rho = −0.14, 95% CI −0.33 to 0.06, p = 0.16 for the Neisse; rho = 0.04, 95% CI −0.13 to 0.21, p = 0.65 for the Neckar main stem) nor the presence of industrial land within the 1 km buffer zone (Cliff’s delta = +0.17, p = 0.14 for the Neisse; delta = −0.01, p = 0.90 for the Neckar main stem) was significantly associated with microplastic levels in either river. Overall, no association between local land cover and surface-water MP concentrations was detectable with the present design; the confidence intervals remain compatible with weak to moderate effects, which this design could not have detected reliably (Section 3.5).

sec.title: 3.4. Influence of WWTPs on MP Contamination
sec.p: Proximity, size, and treatment technology of wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) showed no detectable association with microplastic (MP) concentrations in either catchment (Figure 4). In the Lusatian Neisse, distance to the nearest upstream WWTP displayed a non-significant negative association (Spearman rho = −0.16, 95% CI −0.35 to 0.04, p = 0.11), with near-field sites (<2 km, median 31.0 MP L−1) showing an elevated baseline compared to far-field sites (≥5 km, median 18.0 MP L−1; p = 0.33, Cliff’s delta = +0.14). On the Neckar main stem, distance to the nearest upstream WWTP was not associated with MP concentration (rho = 0.09, 95% CI −0.08 to 0.26, p = 0.30). A positive correlation, i.e., concentrations increasing with distance from the plant, appeared only when the Mannheim samples were included (rho = 0.25, p = 0.001), because 13 of the 15 samples in the > 10 km class came from the confluence and port area, which is not hydraulically connected to the assigned Neckar plants (Figure 4a).

Whether the WWTP treatment level directly drives microplastic levels in the Lusatian Neisse remains uncertain due to overlapping spatial trends. On the one hand, reaches downstream of secondary treatment plants show significantly higher median microplastic concentrations than those near tertiary plants (30.0 vs. 15.0 MP L−1; Mann–Whitney U = 1622, p = 0.011, delta = +0.30). This would be consistent with higher particle loads from the less advanced secondary facilities in the upstream region.

On the other hand, this pattern may be a statistical artifact of spatial location. Secondary plants sit predominantly in the Czech headwaters (mean 25.5 km from source), where overall microplastic levels are higher, while tertiary plants serve the downstream lowland reaches (mean 87.2 km from source). Because plant type and river position overlap, controlling for distance renders the difference between treatment levels non-significant across partial correlation (rho = +0.15, p = 0.13), spatial restriction to the co-occurring reach (p = 0.225), and multivariable regression (p = 0.35).

Neither plant design capacity nor population served correlated with microplastic levels in either river (all |rho| ≤ 0.15, p ≥ 0.13). Fitted separately for each catchment, the negative binomial models (Table 5) showed no detectable association of MP concentration with settlement or industrial share, WWTP distance or population served (all p ≥ 0.11; nonsignificant after Holm adjustment). In the Neisse, the only predictor retained was along-river position, with concentrations decreasing downstream (rate ratio 0.34 per 100 km, 95% CI 0.18–0.61, Holm-adjusted p = 0.002). On the Neckar main stem, the hurdle model fitted better (ΔAIC = 6.1); detection was not associated with any predictor, whereas among the positive samples concentrations increased downstream (rate ratio 1.75 per 100 km, 95% CI 1.25–2.46, Holm-adjusted p = 0.013); a nominal negative association with population served (0.49 per tenfold increase, p = 0.019) did not remain significant after Holm adjustment (p = 0.18). The pooled log-linear model (log10(MP + 1), n = 266 including the Mannheim samples, R2 = 0.12) is not interpreted further: its dominant catchment coefficient restates the difference between the two rivers together with differences in sampling date and hydrological conditions, and its size depended on the constant added before the log transform (0.75 to 0.26 for constants of 0.1 to 10 MP L−1); settlement share was nominally significant only for constants ≤ 1 MP L−1 (p = 0.04–0.05), illustrating the sensitivity to this arbitrary choice (Supplementary Materials).

sec.title: 3.5. Statistical Power, Spatial Dependence and Collector Groups
sec.p: With the available sample sizes, the smallest correlation detectable with 80% power at α = 0.05 is |r| = 0.27 (Pearson) or |rho| = 0.28 (Spearman) for the Neisse (n = 102) and |r| = 0.24 or |rho| = 0.25 for the Neckar main stem (n = 136); if the four continuous land-use and WWTP descriptors of both rivers are treated as one family of eight tests (Bonferroni), these thresholds rise to |rho| = 0.35 and 0.31. Detecting |rho| = 0.2 would require about 205 independent samples per river, and |rho| = 0.1 about 830. These nominal thresholds are optimistic. Because the descriptors are autocorrelated along the river, the effective sample size of the Neisse correlation tests is only 55–68 (minimum detectable |rho| 0.34–0.38). Simulations that include Poisson counting error at the observed particle numbers per bottle (median about 11 in the Neisse and 2.5 in the Neckar) and the observed excess of zeros (13% and 37% beyond the counting model) show that a latent association between a descriptor and the underlying concentration would have to reach about rho = 0.40 in the Neisse and rho = 0.62 in the Neckar to be detected with 80% power. All observed correlations with land-use and WWTP descriptors were weak (|rho| ≤ 0.16 in the Neisse and ≤0.09 in the Neckar), and their 95% confidence intervals exclude strong but not weak-to-moderate associations (largest bounds |rho| = 0.35 and 0.26).

Along the Neisse, log-transformed concentrations showed weak positive spatial autocorrelation at short distances (Moran’s I = 0.22 for neighbors within 2 km, p = 0.014; 0.17 within 5 km, p = 0.009; 0.08 within 10 km, p = 0.03), which was largely explained by the downstream decrease in concentration: with along-river position as covariate, residual autocorrelation was no longer significant (I = 0.13, 0.09 and 0.01; p = 0.09, 0.09 and 0.30), and a GLS model with exponential correlation did not fit better than the independent-error model (likelihood ratio p = 0.17). Weak residual dependence of the negative binomial model between samples less than 2 km apart (I = 0.17, p = 0.04) did not change any conclusion when reach-clustered standard errors were used. Along the Neckar main stem, no positive autocorrelation was detected (I = −0.19, −0.06 and −0.04; p ≥ 0.78). The river comparison was insensitive to along-river dependence (moving-block bootstrap 95% CI for delta 0.29–0.57 with 10 km blocks; medians of 10 km reaches: 20.8 vs. 4.3 MP L−1, U = 459, p < 0.001, delta = 0.64). Moran correlograms and semivariograms are shown in Figure 5.

On the Neckar main stem, concentrations did not differ between samples collected by Wasser 3.0 staff (n = 53; median 5.0 MP L−1; 38% at 0 MP L−1), school and university groups (n = 28; 6.5 MP L−1; 43%) and individual volunteers (n = 49; 5.0 MP L−1; 37%; Kruskal–Wallis H = 0.47, p = 0.79). Seven pairs of co-located samples (≤0.43 km apart, same day) taken by staff and by volunteer or school groups showed no systematic difference (median difference 0 MP L−1; Wilcoxon p = 0.69).

sec.title: 4.1. Comparison with Scientific Monitoring Campaigns Along Rivers
sec.p: Both the Neckar and Neisse datasets display heavily right-skewed distributions characterized by high relative standard deviations and wide inter-percentile ranges (Table 3). Such pronounced positive skewness and extreme dispersion relative to the mean are hallmarks of microplastic distribution in aquatic environments [17]. This variability underlines the dynamic nature of MP distribution, driven by point sources, transport processes and hydrological conditions [17].

Converting the present findings to the standard cubic meter benchmark reveals mean concentrations of about 19,000 MP m−3 (median 5000 MP m−3) for the Neckar main stem and 55,000 MP m−3 (median 23,000 MP m−3) for the Lusatian Neisse, with peak values of about 500,000 and 570,000 MP m−3, respectively.

Due to differing methodologies, comparability with other studies is limited. The advantage of the present approach is the simple 0.5 L grab-sampling procedure, which is fast and can be carried out by volunteers within a citizen-science framework. In addition, the relatively short processing and detection time of 30–40 min per sample enables the analysis of large sample numbers and supports extensive monitoring campaigns [36]. The main limitations are the lack of polymer-specific identification in the detection method and the low sample volumes inherent to grab sampling.

The number of detected MP increases approximately exponentially as the lower size limit of detection decreases [37]. For example, net-trawl studies with a 300–333 µm lower cut-off report concentrations several orders of magnitude lower, such as those conducted in the Laurentian Great Lakes (0.04–0.47 MP m−3, i.e., 0.00004–0.00047 MP L−1) [38]. Even water-column sampling of the Rhine near Basel with a 50 µm lower cut-off yielded a median of only 4.5 MP m−3, which shows that the size threshold alone does not fully reconcile the difference from the present dataset [12].
A study in the North Atlantic found a 10-fold increase in MP abundance when a 100 µm instead of a 500 µm mesh net was used, and a 2.5-fold increase for 100 µm compared with 333 µm [39].

Sturm et al. investigated MP contamination (>10 µm) across three rivers in southwest Germany, the Alb, Queich, and Rehbach, using the same methodology [18]. Overall microplastic concentrations showed high spatial and temporal heterogeneity, ranging from 4 to 1761 MP L−1. Among the three rivers, the Rehbach exhibited the highest average contamination with a mean concentration of 540 ± 476 MP L−1, whereas the Alb recorded the lowest average concentration at 98 ± 54 MP L−1.

Large-volume sampling (100 L) yielded 4.7-fold higher MP recovery and superior reproducibility compared to standard 0.5 L grab sampling [18]. This shows that the sampling volume also affects the MP concentrations determined. A meta-analysis by Cross et al. found decreasing concentrations with increasing sample volumes [40].

Furthermore, because of the small grab-sample volume (0.5 L) and the blank values (Section 2.6), the method cannot detect low MP concentrations. In addition, low-volume grab samples introduce substantial statistical uncertainty because microplastic particles occur as discrete, randomly distributed events in water, which follow a Poisson process [40]. A detection of 2 MP L−1 (one particle in 0.5 L) yields a very wide 95% Poisson interval of roughly 0–6 MP L−1, demonstrating the strong quantization and high relative error at low counts. Even 10 MP L−1 (≈5 particles) still produces a broad interval of about 1–19 MP L−1, whereas 100 MP L−1 (≈50 particles) narrows to approximately 72–128 MP L−1 because Poisson variance increases only with the square root of the count. These examples illustrate that small sample volumes inherently limit precision.

Further, the chosen citizen-science approach provides clear advantages but also has methodological limits. Trained volunteers can greatly expand spatial coverage and reduce monitoring costs and can enable dense, seasonal datasets across entire watersheds [41,42]. Public engagement is an additional benefit. Challenges of citizen-science approaches are variable sample handling, small sample volumes, and the need for expert laboratory validation to ensure data quality. In the present study, samples collected by staff, school and university groups and individual volunteers yielded similar concentrations and shares of non-detects, and co-located samples taken on the same day by different collectors did not differ systematically. These results do not demonstrate equivalence: the number of co-located pairs was small (n = 7), and an equivalence test with a predefined margin was not performed. They do, however, provide no indication of a systematic collector effect exceeding the large natural and counting variability of the data. This supports the use of volunteer-collected grab samples when the sampling procedure is standardized, the samples are georeferenced and checked for plausibility, and processing and analysis are centralized in a laboratory with contamination control (Section 2.2).

sec.title: 4.2. Discussion of Spatio-Temporal Variations
sec.p: In the Mannheim confluence and port area, site means spanned more than an order of magnitude (Table 4), although most of the variance occurred between repeated measurements at the same site (Section 3.2).

A meta-analysis of European freshwater systems found that freshwater microplastic distribution is heavily driven by non-point, episodic mechanisms, primarily storm runoff, atmospheric deposition, and fluctuating hydrological regimes, rather than steady point-source discharges alone [43]. The extreme upper tail observed in both rivers (the maxima of 503 MP L−1 in the Neckar main stem and 569 MP L−1 in the Neisse) may reflect short-lived flush events and localized particle pulses. Because particulate plastics act as non-uniformly suspended matter governed by localized turbulence, settling velocities, and re-suspension thresholds [17], large sample sizes (n > 100) are essential. Small sample sets risk either missing pulse events entirely, thereby underestimating true environmental loads, or overestimating chronic baseline exposure by capturing isolated peak events. Thus, it is recommended to conduct repeated sampling at hotspots to confirm or reject them.

Further, hydrodynamic retention and physical sinks play a pivotal role in the spatial distribution of microplastics. Artificial structures such as lock systems (e.g., Bonadieshafen lock) dramatically reduce flow velocity and alter localized shear stress [44]. Dead zones, impoundments, and stagnant port basins act as physical traps that promote the accumulation and residence time of floating and semi-buoyant microplastics. In addition, localized terrestrial inputs can drive significant spatial variance [17]. Elevated concentrations observed near recycling facilities on the Friesenheimer Insel (167 MP L−1) and industrial terminals near Sandhofen (126 MP L−1) may be caused by localized terrestrial surface runoff and industrial site drainage. This hypothesis requires further investigation of runoff and wastewater streams [45,46].

The difference between sampling points 1 and 2 (Figure 2; Table 4) should also be highlighted; they differ clearly, showing 11 MP L−1 (point 1) and 80 MP L−1 (point 2), despite their close proximity. The reason for this could be the differing flow conditions at the two sampling points. Point 1 is located in the harbor basin, whereas Point 2 is situated in the navigation channel, where stronger currents prevail. It should be noted, however, that the difference is mainly driven by one value of 280 MP L−1 at point 2 (first round); without this value, the means of points 1 and 2 (11 and 14 MP L−1) are almost identical.

In addition to spatial heterogeneity, temporal dynamics dictate environmental risk assessments in these systems. The temporal fluctuations recorded upstream of the Bonadieshafen lock (5 to 1591 MP L−1 between 4 March and 8 April 2026; Section 3.2) illustrate that temporal variation at a single site can exceed the spatial variation between sites; in the port campaign, most of the variance occurred between sampling rounds at the same site and the between-site differences were not statistically significant (Section 3.2). Different studies showed that rainfall events can cause strong increases in MP concentrations by surface runoff [47,48]. Furthermore, changing hydrological conditions can drive settling and resuspension of MP in the riverbed. The hydrological regime of the Lusatian Neisse is itself highly variable: over 1981–2020 the catchment repeatedly experienced multi-month low-flow episodes, and during the 2018–2019 drought discharges fell below the Q70% threshold on more than 55% of days, with individual low-flow periods exceeding 200 days and an annual discharge deficit of up to 86 million m3 at the Przewóz gauge [28]. Such swings in dilution capacity plausibly contribute more to the observed concentration range than the local land-use or wastewater descriptors tested here, and they argue for reporting discharge alongside concentration in future campaigns. The Neckar profile was sampled at water levels close to the long-term mean, whereas the Neisse profile was sampled at below-average water levels (Table 2); a contribution of flow conditions to the difference between the two rivers can therefore not be excluded.

Seasonal variation needs to be considered because the main Neckar sampling was conducted in June (summer), the Neisse in March and May (spring), and the Mannheim port sampling from January to April (winter–spring). Seasonal variations in microplastics in European rivers are mainly driven by changes in hydrological conditions across the year [49,50]. During winter and spring high-flow periods, increased discharge and snowmelt enhance the mobilization and downstream transport of microplastics. In contrast, summer low-flow conditions often lead to reduced transport and temporary accumulation in sediments and near-shore zones. These seasonal patterns show that microplastic dynamics are closely linked to annual fluctuations in flow, precipitation, and catchment hydrology.

Consequently, the Neisse–Neckar difference (H1) should be interpreted as a difference between two campaigns conducted under the respective seasonal and hydrological conditions rather than as a general characteristic of the two catchments; repeated campaigns in both rivers under comparable discharge conditions would be required to separate catchment from seasonal effects.

sec.title: 4.3. Discussion of Land-Use Influence
sec.p: Industrial activities represent major point sources and diffuse drivers of MP contamination in freshwater ecosystems. This applies especially to plastic processing facilities, ranging from polymer manufacturing and plastic recycling plants to heavy manufacturing hubs [45,51,52].

The localized impact of industrial sites is particularly pronounced in industrial ports and manufacturing nodes. In their meta-analysis across European aquatic systems, Hartz et al. concluded that while WWTP proximity influences baseline pollution, concentrated industrial land use and surface runoff from commercial infrastructure create severe local contamination spikes [43]. The magnitude of this potential source is illustrated by direct measurements at a mixed-plastics recycling facility, where raw wash water contained 5.97 × 106 to 1.12 × 108 MP m−3 and the installed 50 µm filtration removed particles above roughly 40 µm efficiently while particles below 10 µm passed through and were discharged, corresponding to an estimated 59–1184 t of microplastic released annually from a single site.

No such proximity effect was detectable in this study; given the minimum detectable effects of the design (Section 3.5), weak to moderate industrial influences cannot be excluded. One reason could be that both rivers flow through densely populated regions with multiple diffuse MP inputs [44]. In combination with the hydrological dynamics of the rivers, this can mask the effects of industry. A comparable mismatch has been reported for the Lake Tollense catchment, where a catchment-scale inventory ranked sub-catchments of 26–219 km2 by emission potential from population, traffic and agriculture, yet the independently measured concentrations corresponded only partly with that ranking: the sub-catchment with the highest agricultural share matched the highest tributary concentrations, whereas the highest lakeshore sediment abundances occurred in a different sub-catchment and spatial differences within the lake itself were not significant [53]. This supports the interpretation that land-use descriptors resolve emission potential rather than the concentration measured at a given point and that the relevant scale is the catchment rather than a 300 m or 1 km riparian buffer [44]. Another explanation could be that MP emissions from the industry present are low because it is largely not plastics-related or because appropriate treatment technologies are applied [54]. Similarly, a watershed-scale citizen-science study found no relationship between MP concentration and land use among sub-watersheds [41].

This could also mask the effect of urbanization on the MP concentration in both rivers. Typically, more strongly urbanized areas show elevated MP concentrations due to surface runoff containing MP [55,56]. Such an effect was not detectable with the present design. It should be emphasized that these null results refer to local descriptors (land cover within 300 m for land use and 1 km for settlements from the sampling point) and to single grab samples; they do not imply that land use is irrelevant as an MP source at the catchment scale, where it is expected to contribute to the diffuse background load measured here.

sec.title: 4.4. Discussion of WWTP Influence
sec.p: WWTP effluents are commonly mentioned as persistent point sources of MP in freshwater systems. Treatment plants retain the majority of the incoming particle load, with reported median removal efficiencies rising from 45.9% after primary to 95.0% after tertiary treatment; because of the high volumetric discharge, however, millions of synthetic fibers and fragments are still released into receiving waters daily [57]. Field investigations comparing riverine MP concentrations upstream and downstream of outfalls confirm a localized impact. Kay et al. (2018) documented significant downstream MP increases across multiple UK rivers following WWTP discharges [58]. Similarly, McCormick et al. observed a sharp rise in downstream MP abundance paired with a distinct shift toward domestic laundry microfibers [59]. While high regional background contamination can occasionally mask effluent inputs in heavily urbanized rivers, targeted upstream–downstream monitoring establishes WWTP outfalls as key drivers of elevated chronic MP loads [60].

With the given study design and applied statistics, no correlation between WWTP upstream distance and MP concentrations could be confirmed. This might be due to the same masking effects that prevented the detection of an influence of industry or population density. The MP concentration might be primarily driven by the hydrological conditions of the rivers. Future monitoring strategies should explicitly account for these hydrological controls by selecting and stratifying sampling sites based on flow conditions and hydrodynamic parameters [44]. Additionally, the ratio between river runoff and WWTP discharge is an important factor for the potential size of the effect, which was not considered here. Because the nearest-plant distance is only a coarse exposure proxy that ignores effluent volume and dilution, and because upstream–downstream pairs at individual outfalls were not sampled, this exploratory screening cannot demonstrate the absence of WWTP inputs. In the Neisse, the higher concentrations downstream of secondary plants coincide with the upper reaches of the river; the apparent treatment-level effect therefore cannot be separated from the longitudinal gradient with the present data (Section 3.4), and a causal attribution to treatment technology is not supported.

sec.title: 4.5. Implications for Future River Monitoring Programs
sec.p: The power analysis and the analysis of spatial dependence (Section 3.5; Figure 5) have direct consequences for the design of future monitoring programs. With about 100–140 single grab samples per river, only moderate to strong associations could be detected reliably (nominally |rho| ≥ 0.25–0.28, and about 0.40 in the Neisse and 0.62 in the Neckar once counting error and excess zeros are taken into account). Weak effects of local land use or wastewater, which are plausible in view of the literature (Section 4.3 and Section 4.4), would require several hundred independent samples or, more efficiently, a lower measurement error per sample through larger volumes or replicate grab samples, which reduce both the Poisson counting error and the share of non-detects (Section 4.1).

Spatial dependence along the rivers was weak. In the Neisse it was confined to distances of a few kilometers and was largely explained by the downstream decrease in concentration. In the Neckar no positive autocorrelation was found (Figure 5). Closely spaced samples therefore contributed largely independent information. Nevertheless, the effective sample size of correlation tests with spatially structured descriptors was reduced (55–68 instead of 102 samples in the Neisse). Future designs should therefore stratify sites by the descriptor of interest, e.g., paired upstream–downstream sites at individual outfalls or contrasting land-use reaches, rather than only increase the density of sites along the river.

Temporal variability must also be addressed explicitly. MP concentrations in rivers depend on discharge and water level, on precipitation and runoff events and on seasonal patterns. Also, the flow regime, which controls the settling, retention and resuspension of particles (Section 4.2), can differ temporally and spatially along the river course due to different flow regimes. In the Mannheim port area, the variation between repeated measurements at the same site exceeded the variation between sites.

Monitoring programs, including the MP monitoring foreseen under the recast Urban Wastewater Treatment Directive, should therefore combine (i) a limited number of fixed sites sampled repeatedly across seasons and water levels, (ii) discharge measurements or gauge data at the time of sampling so that concentrations can be converted into loads and related to the flow regime, and (iii) event-based sampling after precipitation to capture pulse events. Citizen science can provide the sampling density and repetition required for such designs at low cost, whereas sample processing and particle identification remain the limiting factor and require centralized laboratory capacity with trained staff and contamination control.

sec.title: 4.6. Limitations
sec.p: The detection method identifies MP by fluorescence staining and automated particle counting without polymer-specific confirmation. The dye mixture used (abcr eco Wasser 3.0 detect mix MP-1) a mixture of newly developed Nile Red derivatives, which were compared with Nile Red on reference polymers, natural particles and environmental samples and improved the selectivity and precision of detection [61,62]. Nile Red itself also stains natural organic particles with lipophilic surfaces, so false-positive counts are a known problem of Nile Red-based methods [63,64,65]; without additional measures, overestimation by up to 100% has been reported for freshwater samples stained with Nile Red alone [63]. In the present method, the oxidative digestion removes most of the organic matrix, and the validation of the complete procedure reported false-positive rates of 5–6% for wood, chalk and chitin particles together with polymer recoveries of 93–102% [36]. Nevertheless, the reported concentrations are counts of stained particles rather than spectroscopically confirmed polymers. A confirmation of a random subsample by µ-FTIR or Raman spectroscopy is recommended for future campaigns. Because the same protocol was applied to all samples, a residual false-positive rate of this magnitude would affect absolute concentration but is unlikely to explain the relative differences between rivers and sites.

Further limitations concern design. The 0.5 L grab samples imply a large Poisson counting error at low concentrations and a high share of non-detects (Section 4.1); discharge was not measured, and hydrological conditions are characterized only by gauge water levels (Table 2). The two rivers were sampled in different months so that seasonal and catchment differences are confounded; each river was sampled once, which precludes statements on temporal trends outside the Mannheim port area. The spatiotemporal sampling of the Mannheim port area showed profound temporal variations, which are not considered in the monitoring along the river.

Land cover was taken from the CORINE 2018 inventory, and the WWTP descriptors are coarse exposure proxies. Contamination during sampling, transport and storage was not quantified because no field or transport blanks were taken (Section 2.6), and volunteer sampling may have introduced additional, unquantified variability (Section 2.2). Georeferencing via the sampling app was, in a few cases, inconsistent with the time-stamped sampling route.
Given these limitations, the null results for land use and WWTPs indicate that no strong local associations exist under the sampling conditions of this study, but they do not exclude weaker effects.

sec.title: 5. Conclusions
sec.p: This study establishes that, sampled and analyzed with the same protocol, the Lusatian Neisse carried clearly higher concentrations of fluorescently stained MP than the Neckar main stem (H1; Cliff’s delta = 0.44), a difference that is robust to the dataset definition and to spatial dependence between samples. Because the two rivers were sampled in different seasons and at different water levels, this difference characterizes the two campaigns and cannot be attributed to catchment characteristics alone. Concentrations in both rivers were highly skewed, with many non-detects and occasional pulse values. In the Mannheim confluence and port area the temporal variation between repeated measurements at the same site exceeded the variation between sites (H4).

The study cannot establish an influence of local land cover or of WWTP proximity, size or treatment level (H2, H3): no detectable association was found with the given study design, with single 0.5 L grab samples, one campaign per river, no discharge data and coarse exposure proxies. The higher concentrations in the upper Neisse cannot be attributed to the secondary WWTPs located there, because treatment level and longitudinal position are confounded. Due to the single sampling per sampling site, neglecting the strong temporal variations, possible associations and weaker effects cannot be excluded.

The absence of systematic differences between staff, school and volunteer sampling indicates that citizen science can provide the high sample density, provided that sampling is standardized and sample processing is centralized.

For future monitoring programs, we recommend (i) repeated sampling at fixed sites to separate temporal from spatial variation, (ii) larger sample volumes or replicate grabs at low-concentration sites, (iii) recording discharge at the time of sampling, (iv) paired upstream–downstream sampling at individual outfalls, expressed relative to the effluent-to-discharge ratio, (v) sampling across seasons and water levels, including event-based sampling after precipitation, to resolve the dependence of MP concentrations on the flow regime, and (vi) spectroscopic confirmation of a subsample of stained particles (Section 4.5).
